html:
The systematic destruction of the Armenian people of the Ottoman Empire during and after the First World War. Between 600,000 and 1.2 million Armenians were killed, most of them in 1915 and 1916, and Armenian life in Anatolia, some 2,500 years old, came to an end.

Armenians were a Christian minority, protected but second class under Ottoman rule. In the 1890s tens of thousands had already died in the Hamidian massacres. In 1914 the empire, ruled by the nationalist Committee of Union and Progress, entered the First World War and soon lost a winter battle to Russia in the Caucasus. Its leaders blamed Armenians as a disloyal people.

What happened:

  • On 24 April 1915 hundreds of Armenian leaders and writers in Constantinople were arrested and later killed. Armenians mark that date each year.
  • Armenian men were shot or worked to death in labour battalions.
  • Women, children and the old were sent on death marches across Anatolia to the Syrian desert, around Deir ez-Zor, with little food or water. Many were massacred on the way.
  • Tens of thousands of women and children were forcibly converted and taken into Muslim households.

Assyrian and Greek Christians suffered parallel killings at the same time. The survivors scattered to Syria, Lebanon, France, the United States and Soviet Armenia.

The lawyer Raphael Lemkin had these events in mind when he coined the word "genocide" in 1944. Most historians and many states call it genocide. The Republic of Turkey accepts that many Armenians died but rejects the term.
